t: Bitwise OR of All Subsequence Sums
o: We need the OR of the sums of all 2ⁿ subsequences (including the empty one, sum 0). For [2,1,0,3] the achievable sums are 0..6 and their OR is 7. Enumerating subsets is exponential, but there is a striking closed form: the answer equals (OR of all elements) OR (total sum). Intuition: every subset sum's set bits are contained in the bits of total|OR(nums) — a subset sum S satisfies S ≤ total, and if S had a bit above the top structure of total|OR that total lacks, carries would force S > total; conversely every bit of total appears in the full-array sum, and every bit of any single element appears in that singleton's sum, so all bits of total|OR are achieved.
k: Answer = (bitwise OR of all elements) OR (sum of all elements).
Any subset sum's bits are dominated by total|OR(nums), and both operands are themselves achievable subset sums (full set and singletons).

a.i: Compute total = sum(nums) and or = OR of all elements; return total | or. Both values are achievable subset sums (the whole array and each singleton), and no subset sum can have a bit outside total|or: if a subset sum S differed from total first at bit b where S has 1 and total|or has 0, then S would exceed total, impossible.
s: Compute the OR of all elements.

a.i: Maintain the set of all achievable subset sums, extending it element by element; then OR everything. Only feasible for tiny n (sums up to ~1e14 but the set can hold 2ⁿ values), included to validate the closed form experimentally.
s: For each element, add x to every existing sum and union into the set.
Return the OR of all sums.
a.t: O(2ⁿ) — doubles the sum set per element

w: Always submit the O(n) closed form; use the brute force only on paper to trust the claim. Beware overflow: the total can reach 1e14, so use 64-bit integers (in JavaScript, values up to 2⁵³ are safe with regular numbers since n·max = 1e5·1e9 = 1e14 < 9e15). Edge cases: all zeros → 0; single element → that element. Follow-up: OR of all subarray (contiguous) sums — different problem, solvable by observing each prefix sum's contribution.
